In addition, he said, Israel has no desire to hurt the civilian population in Gaza. Lerner said whether to keep the crossings open would be a daily decision. In reality, the truce started breaking down two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza. Since then, dozens of rockets have been fired by Palestinian militants into Israel. Israel Defense Forces said about nine rockets have been launched from Gaza since midnight, pushing the three-day total to more than 110. There are no reports of casualties in Israel. Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak. "Hamas needs to understand that Israel's basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn't mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population," she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. "Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change." Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has threatened to respond to the escalating violence. He warned Hamas again Thursday in an interview on the Al Arabiya television network and seemed to suggest that time was running out. "We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children," Olmert said. "I did not come here to declare war," he continued. "But Hamas must be stopped -- and so it will be. "I will not hesitate to use Israel's strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here."

JERUSALEM (CNN) — A rocket fired by Palestinian militants struck a home in Gaza and killed two children, Palestinian sources said Friday, the same day Israel opened three Gaza border crossings for the first time in 10 days.

A truck carrying grain entered Gaza from Israel on Friday through the Karni crossing point, one of the three crossings Israel reopened.

A third child was in critical condition. The children, all girls and cousins, included the two who died, ages 7 and 12, and the injured child, age 5, Hamas security and Palestinian medical sources said. The rocket struck a house north of Gaza City.

In a separate development, the Israeli military said it allowed a Palestinian who was badly wounded by rocket fire Wednesday to enter Israel for treatment. The Palestinian entered Israel through the Erez Crossing between northern Gaza and Israel.

Israel had closed the crossing except for humanitarian cases because of rocket attacks launched from Gaza into Israel by Palestinian militants. However, it opened three other crossings Friday, allowing fuel and commodities into the Palestinian territory for the first time in more than a week.

About 80 trucks filled with commodities were expected to cross into Gaza. Among the goods were 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas.

The decision to open the crossings at Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz came after requests from international aid groups and Egypt, said Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories. He added that Israel has no desire to harm the civilian population in Gaza.

Lerner said the decision on whether to keep the crossings open would be made on a daily basis.

United Nations assistance programs in Gaza have run out of flour and several essential pharmaceuticals, the U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said.

A tenuous six-month truce between the Hamas government in Gaza and Israel expired a week ago. Under the Egyptian-brokered agreement, Hamas agreed to end militant attacks on Israel from Gaza, while Israel agreed to halt raids inside the territory and ease its blockade on humanitarian goods.

In practice, however, the truce began to unravel two months ago. Rocket attacks by militants became more frequent, and Israel resumed airstrikes inside Gaza.

Since then, dozens of rockets have been fired by Palestinian militants into Israel. The Israel Defense Forces said about nine rockets have been launched from Gaza since midnight, bringing the three-day total to more than 110. There were no reports of casualties in Israel.

The crossings reopened a day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni and Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak met in Cairo, where Egypt expressed concern about the deteriorating humanitarian situation in Gaza.

Livni criticized Hamas after her meeting with Mubarak.

“Hamas needs to understand that Israel’s basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn’t mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population,” she said, according to the Israeli Foreign Ministry. “Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change.”

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has threatened to respond to the escalating violence. He again warned Hamas on Thursday in an interview with the Al Arabiya television network and appeared to suggest that time was running out.

“We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children,” Olmert said.

“I did not come here to declare war,” he continued. “But Hamas must be stopped — and so it will be.

“I will not hesitate to use Israel’s strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here.”

On Friday, a truck loaded with grain crossed from Israel into Gaza at Karni, one of the three reopened crossing points. A third child was critically injured. Hamas security officials and Palestinian medical sources said the children were all girls and cousins: the two who were killed were ages 7 and 12, while the wounded child was 5. The person crossed into Israel through Erez Crossing, which links northern Gaza with Israel. Israel had shut that crossing except for humanitarian cases because of rocket fire from Gaza into Israel by Palestinian militants.

However, on Friday Israel reopened three other crossings, allowing fuel and goods to enter the Palestinian territory for the first time in more than a week. Roughly 80 trucks carrying supplies were expected to pass into Gaza. The shipments included 400,000 liters of fuel and 120 tons of cooking gas.

Peter Lerner, a spokesman for the Coordinator of Government Activities in the Territories, said the decision to reopen Kerem Shalom, Karni and Nahal Oz followed appeals from international aid organizations and Egypt. He added that Israel did not want to harm Gaza’s civilian population. Lerner said the question of whether the crossings would remain open would be reviewed day by day.

The U.N. Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs said United Nations aid programs in Gaza had exhausted their flour supplies and had also run out of several vital medicines.

A fragile six-month cease-fire between Israel and the Hamas government in Gaza ended a week earlier. Under the truce, negotiated by Egypt, Hamas agreed to stop militant attacks launched from Gaza against Israel, while Israel agreed to suspend raids inside Gaza and loosen restrictions on humanitarian supplies.

In practice, the cease-fire had begun to unravel two months earlier. Militant rocket attacks increased, and Israel restarted airstrikes within Gaza. Since then, Palestinian militants have fired dozens of rockets into Israel.

The Israel Defense Forces said around nine rockets had been launched from Gaza since midnight, bringing the total over three days to more than 110. No casualties were reported in Israel.

The crossings reopened one day after Israeli Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni met Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak in Cairo, where Egypt voiced concern over the worsening humanitarian conditions in Gaza.

After meeting Mubarak, Livni condemned Hamas. According to the Israeli Foreign Ministry, she said: “Hamas needs to understand that Israel’s basic desire to live in a tranquil region doesn’t mean that Israel is willing to accept ongoing shooting at its population. Enough is enough. We cannot accept this situation, and the situation will change.”

Israeli Prime Minister Ehud Olmert has warned that Israel may respond to the rising violence. In an interview Thursday with Al Arabiya, he again cautioned Hamas and appeared to indicate that patience was nearing an end.

“We do not want to fight the Palestinian people, but we will not allow Hamas to strike our children,” Olmert said. “I did not come here to declare war,” he added. “But Hamas must be stopped — and so it will be.

“I will not hesitate to use Israel’s strength to strike at Hamas and Islamic Jihad. How? I do not wish to go into details here.”

The incident occurred amid heightened tensions and sporadic exchanges of fire between Palestinian armed groups and Israel. Palestinian health authorities said the children died when the projectile landed in a residential area before reaching Israeli territory. Several others were reported injured.

Aid organizations welcomed the reopening but cautioned that temporary access would not be enough to meet the needs of Gaza’s population, many of whom rely on outside assistance. They urged all parties to protect civilians and ensure that aid can move safely.

counterfactuals.output:
**JERUSALEM —** Israel reopened several border crossings with the Gaza Strip on Sunday to allow humanitarian supplies into the coastal territory, even as officials warned that continued rocket fire by Palestinian militants could prompt a harsher Israeli response following the expiration of a six-month truce with Hamas.

Israeli defense officials said the crossings were opened to permit shipments of food, fuel and other basic goods into Gaza, where aid agencies have warned of worsening shortages after weeks of closures and restrictions. The reopening came after several days of heightened tension along the border, including rocket and mortar fire from Gaza into southern Israel and Israeli warnings that it would not tolerate renewed attacks on its communities.

The truce between Israel and Hamas, which took effect in June, formally expired late last week. Hamas, which controls Gaza, said it would not renew the agreement unless Israel fully lifted its blockade of the territory. Israel said the calm had been repeatedly violated by rocket fire and accused Hamas of using the lull to rearm.

Despite the reopening, humanitarian groups said conditions in Gaza remained severe. The territory’s population depends heavily on imports and international aid, while fuel shortages have affected electricity supplies, water pumping and medical services. Israel has said it allows humanitarian assistance into Gaza but restricts crossings in response to attacks and to prevent weapons smuggling.

Rocket fire continued to be a central flashpoint. Israeli police and military officials reported rockets launched from Gaza toward southern Israel in recent days, sending residents of towns near the border into shelters. There were no immediate reports of major casualties in the latest barrages, but officials said the attacks had disrupted daily life and increased pressure on the government to act.

Foreign Minister Tzipi Livni said Israel could not accept a situation in which its civilians lived under threat from Gaza-based militants. She said Hamas bore responsibility for the deterioration and warned that Israel would respond if attacks continued.

“Israel must protect its citizens,” Livni said in remarks carried by Israeli media. “The responsibility for what happens in Gaza lies with Hamas, and the international community must understand that a terrorist organization cannot be allowed to dictate the lives of people in southern Israel.”

Prime Minister Ehud Olmert also issued a warning to Hamas, saying Israel had shown restraint during the cease-fire but would not remain passive indefinitely. Speaking at a cabinet meeting, Olmert said Israel was seeking to avoid a humanitarian collapse in Gaza while also defending its border communities.

“We are not eager for a confrontation,” Olmert said. “But we will not allow the residents of southern Israel to be targets of continuous rocket fire.”

Hamas officials accused Israel of undermining the truce by maintaining the blockade and carrying out military operations in Gaza. They said the crossings had not been opened sufficiently during the cease-fire and argued that renewed rocket fire was a response to Israeli restrictions and raids.

The cease-fire had brought a relative reduction in violence after months of fighting, though both sides accused the other of violations. Israel says militants continued sporadic rocket launches and exploited the lull to increase their arsenal. Hamas says Israel failed to meet its obligation to ease restrictions on Gaza’s border crossings.

The reopening of the crossings appeared to be a limited move rather than a broader policy shift. Israeli officials said the Kerem Shalom and other crossings could be closed again if rocket attacks persisted. Aid deliveries, they said, would be coordinated with international organizations and subject to security assessments.

The Gaza Strip has been under tightened Israeli and Egyptian restrictions since Hamas seized control of the territory in 2007 after routing forces loyal to Palestinian President Mahmoud Abbas. Israel and Western governments consider Hamas a terrorist organization, while Hamas says it is resisting occupation.

Diplomats have expressed concern that the breakdown of the truce could lead to a larger Israeli military operation in Gaza. Egypt, which helped broker the original cease-fire, has sought to mediate between the sides, but prospects for renewal appeared uncertain as both Israel and Hamas hardened their positions.

For residents on both sides of the border, the end of the lull has revived fears of a wider escalation. In southern Israel, schools and public facilities have reviewed emergency procedures amid repeated sirens. In Gaza, families have stocked up on scarce supplies, worried that another round of closures or fighting could further deepen the humanitarian crisis.

Israeli officials said the coming days would determine whether the situation could be contained. But with the truce expired, rockets continuing and the humanitarian situation in Gaza deteriorating, the fragile calm that had prevailed for much of the previous six months appeared increasingly close to collapse.
